summary: Children aged 6–7 learn to measure in appropriate standard units: length (m/cm), mass (kg/g), temperature (°C) and capacity (litres/ml). The skill has two joined parts: first name the attribute (how long? how heavy? how much fills it? how hot?) so the unit family and instrument match, then choose the grain of unit that yields a readable, precise number (a pencil in cm, not m; a drink in ml, not litres), and read the instrument to the nearest sensible mark.
misconceptions: Uses a unit or tool from the wrong attribute — e.g. reaches for a ruler to find 'how much water', or gives grams for a length.
Picks the wrong grain — measures a pencil in metres ('0 m') or a room laboriously in centimetres — not choosing to the nearest appropriate unit.
Happily reports a non-standard count ('6 cubes') when a standard measurement is asked for, not seeing why standard units matter.
Reads the instrument carelessly — doesn't measure to the nearest mark, mis-reads the jug's meniscus or the scale.

activities.title: Measuring station: choose the tool and the unit
steps: Set out a mixed set of objects one at a time — a pencil, a table, an apple, a jug of juice, a cup of water (and, if available, something whose temperature matters) — with a ruler/tape, a kitchen scale, a measuring jug and a thermometer all available.
For each object, first say out loud what KIND of measurement this is: how long? how heavy? how much fills it? how hot?
Pick the matching instrument, then choose the standard unit (m or cm, kg or g, litres or ml, °C).
Measure to the nearest mark and state the amount with its unit.

Try a deliberate mismatch — measure the pencil in metres — and notice the number is useless (to the nearest metre a pencil rounds to '0 m'); then switch to centimetres and get a clean reading (a real pencil is usually somewhere between about 10 cm and 19 cm, depending on how much it has been sharpened).
Try reaching for the ruler to measure the jug of juice and notice it cannot give a capacity reading at all.
activities.insight: You first decide what kind of quantity you are measuring so the unit family and tool fit, then choose a unit grain that gives a sensible, readable number.

activities.title: Why standard units at all — the hand-span contrast
steps: Measure the same object (e.g. a table) in hand-spans with two different people and record both counts — for example one person gets 8, another gets 9.
Discuss why the two counts differ for the same table.
Re-measure with a ruler in centimetres and compare: everyone gets the same number.
Explain in your own words why we use standard units like centimetres instead of hand-spans or cubes.
activities.insight: Standard units let everyone agree and compare, because a non-standard unit changes from person to person.

activities.title: Sort objects to their sensible unit
steps: Sort a set of everyday objects under the unit you would use: m, cm, kg, g, litres, ml, °C.
Answer targeted questions such as 'Which unit would you use to weigh an apple?' and justify the choice, rejecting a too-big option like kilograms in favour of grams.
Pair each unit with a benchmark object (a metre stick, a 1 kg bag, a 1 litre bottle) and use the benchmark to sanity-check your sorting.
activities.insight: Each attribute and each sensible size has a matching unit family and grain, which a benchmark size helps you judge.

activities.title: Benchmark reference card
steps: Keep a reference chart beside your measuring that pairs each unit with a benchmark size and example objects (a metre stick for m, a 1 kg bag for kg, a 1 litre bottle for litres).
Reveal each pairing and use it to check whether your chosen unit looks right for the object in front of you.
activities.insight: Anchoring each unit to a familiar benchmark size helps you judge which unit gives a readable number.

activities.title: Read the instrument to the nearest mark
steps: With the correct tool and unit already chosen, read a ruler, scale, measuring jug and thermometer carefully.
Read the measuring jug at eye level and find the liquid line (meniscus).
Round to the nearest marked line rather than guessing a whole number.
State the measurement precisely with its unit.
activities.insight: Even with the right tool and unit, the reading must be taken to the nearest mark and from the correct line to be accurate.

checkQuestion: Lay out a range of objects — a pencil, a table, an apple, a jug of juice, a cup of water (and, if you have one, something whose temperature matters) — with a ruler and tape, a scale, a measuring jug and a thermometer available. Say: 'Measure each of these and tell me the amount.' Do not tell them which tool or unit. Watch which instrument and unit they reach for, whether the grain fits, and how they read it.
checkAnswer: For each object the child identifies the attribute and selects a matching instrument, chooses a standard unit of an appropriate grain (cm for the pencil, m for the table/room, g for the apple, ml for the cup, litres for the jug), measures to the nearest unit, and states the amount with its unit — and can say why that unit rather than a much bigger or smaller one.
